exam: A child from a malaria‑endemic area presents with fever, seizures and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9 – what is your immediate management and why? — Give IV artesunate, secure airway, treat raised ICP; explain malaria’s role.

You obtain a CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and high protein in a HIV‑positive child – what diagnoses are top on your list and how would you confirm? — Consider cryptococcal meningitis and CMV; order India‑ink stain or cryptococcal antigen, PCR for CMV.

A 7‑year‑old with chronic otitis media develops focal seizures and a fever – what imaging would you request and what finding would change treatment? — Request CT/MRI; a ring‑enhancing lesion indicates abscess requiring drainage and antibiotics.

Why is ceftriaxone combined with metronidazole for suspected brain abscess in low‑resource settings? — Ceftriaxone covers streptococci and gram‑negatives; metronidazole adds anaerobic coverage common in sinus/ear sources.

A child on antiretroviral therapy develops headache and visual loss; CSF shows low glucose – which organism is most likely and what drug regimen is avoided? — Cryptococcus neoformans; avoid fluconazole monotherapy in severe disease, use amphotericin B + flucytosine.
Explain how you would assess for raised intracranial pressure when CT is unavailable. — Look for bulging fontanelle, vomiting, papilledema, and use optic nerve sheath ultrasound if possible.

What preventive measures reduce the incidence of non‑typical CNS infections in this region? — Insecticide‑treated nets, early malaria treatment, vaccination, HIV testing and treatment, and prompt management of ear infections.

How does neurocysticercosis present differently from cerebral malaria, and what key test distinguishes them? — Seizures without severe systemic illness; brain imaging shows calcified cysts versus normal imaging in malaria.
ai.title: Other Central Nervous System Infections in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A review of less common paediatric CNS infections seen in low‑resource settings, focusing on clinical reasoning, diagnosis, and management without relying on advanced tests.

b: Identify infection by fever, altered consciousness, focal neurologic signs, or seizures.
CSF: pleocytosis with lymphocyte predominance, normal or mildly low glucose, protein elevation.
sections.p: Any infection of the brain, spinal cord or meninges that is not classic bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis or tuberculous meningitis. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and basic CSF analysis.

t.b: Is there an inflammatory CSF? – Presence of cells, protein rise, glucose drop confirms infection.
Is malaria contributing? – Positive test directs antimalarial therapy even if CSF is abnormal.
Is immunosuppression present? – Positive result raises suspicion for opportunistic CNS infections.

b: Mild: alert, no seizures, normal vitals.
Moderate: irritability, single seizure, mild tachypnoea.
Severe: coma, recurrent seizures, respiratory failure.
sections.p: Use the WHO Paediatric Meningitis Severity Score: consciousness level, seizures, bulging fontanelle, and respiratory distress.

b: Cerebral malaria (Plasmodium falciparum).
HIV‑related opportunistic infections (CMV, cryptococcus).
Bacterial brain abscess from otitis media or sinusitis (Staphylococcus, anaerobes).
Fungal infections (Candida, Histoplasma).
Parasitic infections (Neurocysticercosis, schistosomiasis).
sections.p: In East Africa, the common non‑typical CNS pathogens are:

b: Cerebral malaria: fever, seizures, coma, papilledema.
Brain abscess: focal headache, vomiting, focal deficit, fever.
Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV): subacute headache, neck stiffness, visual changes.
Neurocysticercosis: seizures, focal deficits, calcified lesions on imaging.
sections.p: Presentation varies with pathogen and location of infection.

b: Fundoscopy for papilledema.
Basic CSF analysis.
sections.p: Prioritise bedside tools; use imaging only when available.

t.a: Point‑of‑care ultrasound of optic nerve sheath
t.b: If unavailable, rely on clinical signs (bulging fontanelle, vomiting).
If unavailable, treat empirically based on likely source (e.g., otitis media).

b: Rapidly decreasing consciousness.
Recurrent seizures despite treatment.
Signs of brain herniation (bradycardia, irregular breathing).
Persistent fever >48 h after therapy.
Cerebral malaria: IV artesunate (first‑line), avoid quinine toxicity.
Brain abscess: high‑dose IV ceftriaxone + metronidazole; surgical drainage if >2 cm or mass effect.
Cryptococcal meningitis: IV amphotericin B + flucytosine; avoid fluconazole monotherapy in severe disease.
Neurocysticercosis: albendazole + steroids; avoid steroids alone.
sections.p: Treat the underlying pathogen, control ICP, and prevent secondary injury.

b: Repeat CSF if no clinical improvement after 48 h.
Vaccinate against Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcus to reduce secondary bacterial CNS infection.
Provide insecticide‑treated nets and prompt malaria treatment.
sections.p: Monitor neurologic recovery and address underlying risk factors.

b: Classic bacterial meningitis – differs by CSF neutrophil predominance and rapid progression.
Acute encephalitis – usually viral, with normal CSF glucose and less focal mass effect.
Normal CSF glucose in early cerebral malaria may give false reassurance.
Negative malaria rapid test does not exclude low‑parasite‑density infection; consider thick smear.

whenToSeekHelp: Loss of consciousness, persistent seizures, signs of brain herniation, or rapid deterioration.
